question: A colleague new to Claude at work asks why anyone would use the default tier when a deeper-reasoning one is offered alongside it. Which explanation is accurate?
options: A) The default tier exists to hold costs down and produces work that is noticeably weaker than the deeper tier on every kind of task attempted.
B) The default tier is the quickest and cheapest option available, and it is intended for very high volumes of short, repetitive requests.
C) The default tier is fast and capable enough for most everyday work, so the deeper tier's greater allowance cost is worth paying only when depth decides it.
D) The default tier is intended for people who are still learning to use Claude, and experienced colleagues are generally expected to move up once they feel confident.
correct_answers: C) The default tier is fast and capable enough for most everyday work, so the deeper tier's greater allowance cost is worth paying only when depth decides it.
explanations: This understates the default badly. It is a capable tier that handles most everyday work well; the difference in reasoning depth shows on genuinely hard problems, not uniformly across every task.
This describes the lightest tier rather than the default. Being fastest and cheapest for very high-volume short requests is a different position in the range from the general-purpose default.

Correct. The default is fast and capable and suits the majority of work, while the deepest tier consumes meaningfully more allowance, so it is reserved for tasks where reasoning depth changes the outcome.
Tier choice tracks the demands of the task, not the experience of the user. An expert doing routine drafting is well served by the default, and a beginner facing a hard analysis may need more depth.
